Console tables for Japandi design work best when they combine the clean lines of Scandinavian minimalism with the warmth and craftsmanship of Japanese aesthetics — think natural wood, slender legs, a low profile, and absolutely nothing unnecessary on the surface. The right piece grounds your entryway or living room in calm without looking sparse or cold.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in your hallway, staring at a console table that just doesn't feel right — too bulky, too shiny, too "nothing" — and wondered what on earth would actually suit the calm, intentional look you're going for? I ask because I've been there myself, and so have most of my clients. The answer almost always lives at the intersection of considered furniture choice and the wall art and decor you arrange around it.

Quick answer: Japandi console tables are typically low-profile, made from natural wood (like oak, ash or walnut), and styled with minimal clutter. Pair them with neutral-toned wall art, a single ceramic piece, and soft organic textiles to complete the look without overdoing it.

Japandi is a design philosophy that blends the best of Japanese wabi-sabi living — the beauty of imperfection, natural materials, and quiet restraint — with the hygge-influenced cosiness and functionality of Scandinavian interiors. It's one of the most liveable, genuinely calming styles you can bring into a home, and a console table is often the first piece that sets the tone. If you want to pull the full look together, pairing your furniture with unique wall art and thoughtfully chosen unique home decor makes all the difference between a vignette that works and one that just sort of sits there.

What Are Japandi Console Tables?

A Japandi console table is any narrow, flat-topped table that follows the core principles of Japandi design: natural materials, clean geometry, low-to-mid height, and no decorative excess. The look is minimal but never cold — there's always something tactile or organic about it.

What separates a Japandi piece from a generic Scandi one is the attention to craft. Joints might be slightly visible, the grain of the wood is meant to be appreciated, and the overall proportions feel considered rather than simply modern.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A light-filled Japanese-Scandinavian entryway with a low solid-oak console table on slender tapered legs, bare except for a single round ceramic bowl and a small dried-pampas arrangement. Behind it, a raw plaster wall with a wooden wall shelf holding a small woven basket. The floor is pale wide-board timber. A South Asian woman in her thirties stands beside the table, casually arranging the ceramic bowl in a natural candid pose, wearing a soft beige linen outfit.]]

Core Characteristics of a Japandi Console Table

  • Natural solid wood — oak, walnut, ash or bamboo preferred
  • Slender tapered or straight legs, often with visible joinery
  • Low-to-mid height (typically 75–85 cm)
  • Minimal or zero ornamentation
  • Matte or oil-rubbed finishes, never high gloss
  • Occasional open lower shelf for a single decorative object
  • Neutral or warm-toned colour — no painted bright colours
Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether a console table reads as Japandi, turn it around in your mind: would it look at home in a Japanese tea house AND a Danish living room? If yes, you're on the right track.

How To Choose a Japandi Console Table

Choosing the right console table for Japandi design comes down to four things: material, proportion, finish, and how it relates to the wall behind it. Get those right and the rest of the styling becomes much easier.

I always tell clients to measure the wall width before anything else. A console that's too wide makes the space feel squeezed; too narrow and it floats awkwardly. A good rule is 60–75% of the wall width for an entryway, slightly more relaxed for a living room.

Add four bullet labels pointing to the key differences: material, leg style, finish, and height proportion.]]

What to Look For When Buying

  • Material: Solid wood beats veneers every time — look for oak, walnut or ash
  • Leg style: Tapered, square or hairpin legs all work; avoid turned or carved ornate legs
  • Height: Match roughly to a standard door handle height or slightly lower
  • Width: Leave at least 20 cm breathing room on each side from the wall edge
  • Finish: Oiled, waxed or natural — avoid lacquered or high-sheen finishes
  • Storage: A single lower shelf adds function without visual clutter
  • Joinery: Visible dovetail or mortise joints are a bonus — they signal quality craft

I once helped a client who'd bought a beautiful walnut console — genuinely lovely piece — but it sat 95 cm tall, which is quite high for the low-ceilinged Victorian hallway she had. It made the whole space feel top-heavy. We swapped it for a lower ash alternative and the hall immediately breathed. Height really does matter more than people realise.

Pro Tip: If you're shopping in person, bring a swatch of your wall colour or flooring. Japandi relies on tonal harmony — a wood that clashes with your floor will fight the whole scheme no matter how beautiful it is on its own.

Styling Your Japandi Console Table

Styling a Japandi console table is about restraint with intention — every object on the surface should earn its place, and there should be noticeable negative space (empty surface) as part of the composition. This is where most people go wrong: they fill it up because empty space feels unfinished. It isn't.

Think in odd numbers and vary the heights of objects. A low ceramic vase, a mid-height candle or twig arrangement, and a trailing plant at one end create a natural diagonal rhythm that draws the eye without overwhelming.

[[IMG|styling-japandi-console-table|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A styled Japandi console table in a living room corner, topped with three objects: a short round stoneware vase with a single dried stem, a beeswax pillar candle on a flat stone holder, and a small trailing pothos plant in a terracotta pot at one end. The surface is mostly clear. A simple woven wall sconce hangs above. A Black British woman in her late twenties crouches slightly to adjust the plant, candid and natural, wearing a cream oversized knit.]]

The Japandi Console Styling Formula

  • Keep at least 50% of the surface clear — negative space is intentional, not lazy
  • Use three objects maximum: one low, one mid, one taller or trailing
  • Stick to natural textures: stone, ceramic, linen, dried botanicals, unvarnished wood
  • Avoid anything reflective, metallic or brightly coloured on the surface
  • Add one living element — a plant or fresh stem — to bring warmth and life
  • A small tray in natural rattan or slate keeps keys and everyday items contained
  • Soft ambient lighting via a slim table lamp ties the vignette together after dark
[[PRODUCT|small ceramic stoneware vase for Japandi console decor]]
Real Example: A client of mine tried to style her console with five objects and it looked cluttered. We removed two, shifted the remaining three to the left-hand two-thirds of the surface, and suddenly it looked intentional and calm. The lesson? Edit harder than you think you need to.

Japandi Console Table Variations and Features

Not all Japandi console tables are identical — there's actually a useful range of variations depending on your storage needs, room size, and personal lean towards the Scandi or Japanese end of the aesthetic. Knowing the differences helps you choose a piece that genuinely works for your home rather than just looking pretty on a website.

The most common variation is the shelf console — a single low open shelf below the main surface. It's brilliant for a hallway because you can store a basket of scarves there or a pair of slippers without breaking the visual calm of the top surface.

Pro Tip: If your hallway is narrower than 120 cm, go for a wall-mounted floating console. It gives you the look without eating into the walking space — and it makes the floor feel longer.

Wall Art and Decor Pairings Above a Japandi Console Table

The wall above your console table is genuinely as important as the table itself — possibly more so. It's the first thing the eye travels to when you walk into a room, and if it's bare or wrong, even a perfect console table will feel unfinished.

For Japandi, the wall above should be calm and considered. Think one strong piece of art rather than a gallery wall, a single mirror with a simple frame, or an organic wall-hanging. Busy gallery walls are firmly in the maximalist camp and will undercut the whole aesthetic.

A woman of East Asian heritage in her forties stands slightly to the side, glancing up at the mirror arrangement with a relaxed thoughtful expression, wearing a sage linen shirt.]]

Best Wall Art and Decor Options for a Japandi Console

  • Abstract botanical prints — ink-wash or watercolour styles in earth tones or sumi-e (Japanese ink) look outstanding
  • Single large-format art print — one piece, centred, roughly two-thirds the width of the console below it
  • Round or arch-top mirror — adds light and softness without visual noise
  • Woven macramé or tapestry panel — textural, organic, very much in keeping with wabi-sabi
  • Simple wooden wall shelf above — hold a single object and leave space around it
  • Wall-mounted branch or dried botanical — brings nature indoors in the most pared-back way
  • Framed calligraphy or kanji-style text art — if kept to one piece in black on cream, it's quietly beautiful

The most common mistake I see here is hanging the art too high. I visited a client's flat once where a lovely abstract print was hung almost at ceiling height above the console — it looked like it was floating away from everything below it. Dropped it down so the bottom of the frame sat about 25 cm above the console surface and the whole vignette clicked into place immediately.

[[PRODUCT|abstract botanical wall art prints in earth tones for Japandi styling]] [[PRODUCT|Japanese ink-wash landscape artwork for entryway wall]]
Pro Tip: When choosing art for above a console table, aim for the bottom of the frame to sit roughly 20–30 cm above the table surface. Any higher and the art disconnects from the furniture below; any lower and it feels cramped.

Colour Palette Guidance for Japandi Entryway Vignettes

Getting the colour palette right is honestly what separates a convincing Japandi entryway from one that just has a wooden table in it. The palette is deceptively simple — but there's more going on than pure white and beige.

Japandi colour sits in a narrow band: warm off-whites, stone, clay, sage, charcoal, dusty terracotta, and the natural tones of wood and linen. What you're avoiding is anything that shouts — no bright whites, no saturated colours, no cool greys without warmth in them.

A Japandi entryway styled in a warm palette of stone, clay and warm off-white. Walls are clay-lime plaster, the console is ash wood with a natural oil finish. A terracotta ceramic pot with a green trailing plant sits at one end of the console. A round jute wall hanging adds texture to the wall. A Middle Eastern man in his fifties stands near the console, hands in pockets, looking relaxed and at ease in the space, wearing a soft charcoal linen jacket.]]

Japandi Entryway Colour Palette by Layer

  • Wall colour: Warm off-white, raw plaster tone, pale stone or dusty sage — avoid cool or blue-toned whites
  • Floor: Pale to mid-tone timber, natural stone tiles, or warm-toned concrete
  • Console wood tone: Light ash or oak for a Scandi lean; darker walnut for a more Japanese feel
  • Accent colours: One or two only — muted terracotta, dusty sage or deep charcoal
  • Art and textiles: Cream, warm white, tan, sand, ink black — echo the wall and wood tones
  • Avoid: Bright white walls, cool grey tones, navy, mustard or any saturated colour
Real Example: I worked with a couple who'd painted their hallway a stark brilliant white, then wondered why their beautiful oak console looked slightly cold. We repainted in a warm stone-white — just a touch of yellow and grey in the pigment — and the wood suddenly looked alive. The room hadn't changed; the background had.

Budget vs Premium Japandi Console Table Options

Here's something I appreciate about Japandi design: the aesthetic actually rewards restraint in budget as much as it rewards craftsmanship at the higher end. You genuinely don't need to spend a fortune if you know what to prioritise.

The key is knowing where to invest and where to save. I'd always put money into the table itself over the styling objects — a well-made solid wood piece will outlast trends and take on a better patina over time. The decor around it can be budget-friendly and still look curated.

Where to Spend vs Where to Save

  • Spend on: Solid wood table, quality joinery, a well-made piece of wall art above it
  • Save on: Ceramic vessels from supermarkets or charity shops, dried botanicals from a florist's offcuts
  • Budget table tip: A plain pine or rubberwood table painted with a chalk-finish paint in a warm neutral reads surprisingly well in Japandi settings
  • Premium table tip: Solid walnut with hand-finished oil and exposed tenon joints is the gold standard — worth the investment if your hallway is a focal space
  • Mid-range sweet spot: Solid oak from Scandinavian furniture chains hits quality without premium pricing
  • Art investment: One well-chosen art print above a budget console transforms the whole vignette — this is worth spending on
[[PRODUCT|minimalist Japandi wall art print for entryway styling]]
Pro Tip: If budget is tight, start with a solid secondhand table from a vintage market — older Scandi furniture from the 60s and 70s is practically Japandi-ready as it is — and invest in one quality piece of art for the wall above it. That combination will look far more intentional than a cheap new table with a bare wall.

DIY Japandi Console Table Styling Tips with Accessible Decor

You don't need a stylist's budget or access to niche design boutiques to create a convincing Japandi console vignette. Most of the best pieces in this look are things you can find in garden centres, charity shops, supermarkets, or even in your own garden.

I've done entire console table setups for clients using items that cost less than twenty pounds total, and they've photographed beautifully. The trick is always in the edit — choosing a few genuinely nice things and giving them space to breathe rather than crowding the surface.

A DIY Japandi console table styled with accessible items: a supermarket ceramic mug repurposed as a vase holding a single eucalyptus stem, a flat river pebble as a candle holder, and a folded beige linen cloth draped at one end. The table is a simple pale wood piece. A hanging plant in a macramé hanger is visible on the wall above. A young woman of mixed British-Caribbean heritage crouches beside the table, arranging a small stem in the ceramic vessel with a focused, relaxed expression.]]

DIY Styling Sources and Swaps

  • Vessels: Plain supermarket ceramic mugs, jars, or small bowls work beautifully as vases — choose cream, terracotta or stone tones
  • Botanicals: Dried pampas, eucalyptus, or even garden twigs in winter add organic texture for almost nothing
  • Trays: A piece of flat slate, a chopping board, or a folded linen cloth corrals smaller items tidily
  • Candles: Cream beeswax pillar candles from food shops or pound stores hit the Japandi palette perfectly
  • Wall decor: A large round mirror from a charity shop, spray-painted matte black or left natural, reads as intentional
  • Plants: A single pothos, spider plant or small olive tree in a terracotta pot is Japandi at its most honest
  • Art: Print a botanical ink-wash image at home in black and white and frame it in a simple raw wood frame
[[PRODUCT|wabi-sabi style nature wall art prints for budget Japandi styling]] [[PRODUCT|woven jute or rattan decorative tray for console table]]
Pro Tip: The single most accessible DIY upgrade for a Japandi console is a plain terracotta pot with a trailing plant, placed at one end of the surface. It costs a few pounds, brings life and warmth, and immediately makes the arrangement feel intentional rather than accidental.

What the Experts Say About Japandi Design

Japandi has moved well beyond trend status — it's becoming one of the defining residential interior styles of the decade, and it's easy to see why when you understand what it's actually doing for people's sense of calm at home.

The philosophy at its heart is about reducing visual noise without reducing warmth. That's the balance that makes Japandi so liveable compared to pure minimalism, which can feel cold and aspirational in a way that's exhausting to maintain day to day.

If you want to read more about the history and principles behind the style, Japandi Style: Everything You Need to Know About These East-Meets-West Interiors from Architectural Digest is a genuinely useful deep read — it explains the wabi-sabi and hygge connections in a way that gives you real context for your decor decisions.

The practical upshot for console table styling is this: Japandi design rewards permanence over trend-chasing. The table, the art above it, the ceramic on the surface — buy these things carefully and they'll work just as well in fifteen years as they do today.

Let's Keep the Conversation Going

Creating a Japandi console table vignette really is one of the most satisfying things you can do for a home — it's focused, achievable, and the result is a corner of your space that genuinely feels considered and calm every single day you walk past it.

Whether you're starting from scratch with a new table or working with something you already own, the principles are the same: natural materials, a restrained surface, one strong piece on the wall above, and a palette that borrows warmth from wood and nature rather than from colour.

You don't need to do it all at once either. Start with the table and one object. Then add the art. Then refine from there. The best Japandi spaces I've ever seen were built slowly over time, not installed in a weekend.

So — what does your current entryway or console table situation look like, and what's the one thing you'd most like to change about it first?

  • Natural solid wood — oak, walnut, ash or bamboo preferred
  • Slender tapered or straight legs, often with visible joinery
  • Low-to-mid height (typically 75–85 cm)
  • Minimal or zero ornamentation
  • Matte or oil-rubbed finishes, never high gloss
  • Occasional open lower shelf for a single decorative object
  • Neutral or warm-toned colour — no painted bright colours
Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether a console table reads as Japandi, turn it around in your mind: would it look at home in a Japanese tea house AND a Danish living room? If yes, you're on the right track.

How To Choose a Japandi Console Table

Choosing the right console table for Japandi design comes down to four things: material, proportion, finish, and how it relates to the wall behind it. Get those right and the rest of the styling becomes much easier.

I always tell clients to measure the wall width before anything else. A console that's too wide makes the space feel squeezed; too narrow and it floats awkwardly. A good rule is 60–75% of the wall width for an entryway, slightly more relaxed for a living room.

What to Look For When Buying

  • Material: Solid wood beats veneers every time — look for oak, walnut or ash
  • Leg style: Tapered, square or hairpin legs all work; avoid turned or carved ornate legs
  • Height: Match roughly to a standard door handle height or slightly lower
  • Width: Leave at least 20 cm breathing room on each side from the wall edge
  • Finish: Oiled, waxed or natural — avoid lacquered or high-sheen finishes
  • Storage: A single lower shelf adds function without visual clutter
  • Joinery: Visible dovetail or mortise joints are a bonus — they signal quality craft

I once helped a client who'd bought a beautiful walnut console — genuinely lovely piece — but it sat 95 cm tall, which is quite high for the low-ceilinged Victorian hallway she had. It made the whole space feel top-heavy. We swapped it for a lower ash alternative and the hall immediately breathed. Height really does matter more than people realise.

Pro Tip: If you're shopping in person, bring a swatch of your wall colour or flooring. Japandi relies on tonal harmony — a wood that clashes with your floor will fight the whole scheme no matter how beautiful it is on its own.

Styling Your Japandi Console Table

Styling a Japandi console table is about restraint with intention — every object on the surface should earn its place, and there should be noticeable negative space (empty surface) as part of the composition. This is where most people go wrong: they fill it up because empty space feels unfinished. It isn't.

Think in odd numbers and vary the heights of objects. A low ceramic vase, a mid-height candle or twig arrangement, and a trailing plant at one end create a natural diagonal rhythm that draws the eye without overwhelming.

The Japandi Console Styling Formula

  • Keep at least 50% of the surface clear — negative space is intentional, not lazy
  • Use three objects maximum: one low, one mid, one taller or trailing
  • Stick to natural textures: stone, ceramic, linen, dried botanicals, unvarnished wood
  • Avoid anything reflective, metallic or brightly coloured on the surface
  • Add one living element — a plant or fresh stem — to bring warmth and life
  • A small tray in natural rattan or slate keeps keys and everyday items contained
  • Soft ambient lighting via a slim table lamp ties the vignette together after dark

Japandi Console Table Variations and Features

Not all Japandi console tables are identical — there's actually a useful range of variations depending on your storage needs, room size, and personal lean towards the Scandi or Japanese end of the aesthetic. Knowing the differences helps you choose a piece that genuinely works for your home rather than just looking pretty on a website.

The most common variation is the shelf console — a single low open shelf below the main surface. It's brilliant for a hallway because you can store a basket of scarves there or a pair of slippers without breaking the visual calm of the top surface.

Wall Art and Decor Pairings Above a Japandi Console Table

The wall above your console table is genuinely as important as the table itself — possibly more so. It's the first thing the eye travels to when you walk into a room, and if it's bare or wrong, even a perfect console table will feel unfinished.

For Japandi, the wall above should be calm and considered. Think one strong piece of art rather than a gallery wall, a single mirror with a simple frame, or an organic wall-hanging. Busy gallery walls are firmly in the maximalist camp and will undercut the whole aesthetic.

Best Wall Art and Decor Options for a Japandi Console

  • Abstract botanical prints — ink-wash or watercolour styles in earth tones or sumi-e (Japanese ink) look outstanding
  • Single large-format art print — one piece, centred, roughly two-thirds the width of the console below it
  • Round or arch-top mirror — adds light and softness without visual noise
  • Woven macramé or tapestry panel — textural, organic, very much in keeping with wabi-sabi
  • Simple wooden wall shelf above — hold a single object and leave space around it
  • Wall-mounted branch or dried botanical — brings nature indoors in the most pared-back way
  • Framed calligraphy or kanji-style text art — if kept to one piece in black on cream, it's quietly beautiful

The most common mistake I see here is hanging the art too high. I visited a client's flat once where a lovely abstract print was hung almost at ceiling height above the console — it looked like it was floating away from everything below it. Dropped it down so the bottom of the frame sat about 25 cm above the console surface and the whole vignette clicked into place immediately.

Colour Palette Guidance for Japandi Entryway Vignettes

Getting the colour palette right is honestly what separates a convincing Japandi entryway from one that just has a wooden table in it. The palette is deceptively simple — but there's more going on than pure white and beige.

Japandi colour sits in a narrow band: warm off-whites, stone, clay, sage, charcoal, dusty terracotta, and the natural tones of wood and linen. What you're avoiding is anything that shouts — no bright whites, no saturated colours, no cool greys without warmth in them.

Japandi Entryway Colour Palette by Layer

  • Wall colour: Warm off-white, raw plaster tone, pale stone or dusty sage — avoid cool or blue-toned whites
  • Floor: Pale to mid-tone timber, natural stone tiles, or warm-toned concrete
  • Console wood tone: Light ash or oak for a Scandi lean; darker walnut for a more Japanese feel
  • Accent colours: One or two only — muted terracotta, dusty sage or deep charcoal
  • Art and textiles: Cream, warm white, tan, sand, ink black — echo the wall and wood tones
  • Avoid: Bright white walls, cool grey tones, navy, mustard or any saturated colour
Real Example: I worked with a couple who'd painted their hallway a stark brilliant white, then wondered why their beautiful oak console looked slightly cold. We repainted in a warm stone-white — just a touch of yellow and grey in the pigment — and the wood suddenly looked alive. The room hadn't changed; the background had.

Budget vs Premium Japandi Console Table Options

Here's something I appreciate about Japandi design: the aesthetic actually rewards restraint in budget as much as it rewards craftsmanship at the higher end. You genuinely don't need to spend a fortune if you know what to prioritise.

The key is knowing where to invest and where to save. I'd always put money into the table itself over the styling objects — a well-made solid wood piece will outlast trends and take on a better patina over time. The decor around it can be budget-friendly and still look curated.

Where to Spend vs Where to Save

  • Spend on: Solid wood table, quality joinery, a well-made piece of wall art above it
  • Save on: Ceramic vessels from supermarkets or charity shops, dried botanicals from a florist's offcuts
  • Budget table tip: A plain pine or rubberwood table painted with a chalk-finish paint in a warm neutral reads surprisingly well in Japandi settings
  • Premium table tip: Solid walnut with hand-finished oil and exposed tenon joints is the gold standard — worth the investment if your hallway is a focal space
  • Mid-range sweet spot: Solid oak from Scandinavian furniture chains hits quality without premium pricing
  • Art investment: One well-chosen art print above a budget console transforms the whole vignette — this is worth spending on

DIY Japandi Console Table Styling Tips with Accessible Decor

You don't need a stylist's budget or access to niche design boutiques to create a convincing Japandi console vignette. Most of the best pieces in this look are things you can find in garden centres, charity shops, supermarkets, or even in your own garden.

I've done entire console table setups for clients using items that cost less than twenty pounds total, and they've photographed beautifully. The trick is always in the edit — choosing a few genuinely nice things and giving them space to breathe rather than crowding the surface.

DIY Styling Sources and Swaps

  • Vessels: Plain supermarket ceramic mugs, jars, or small bowls work beautifully as vases — choose cream, terracotta or stone tones
  • Botanicals: Dried pampas, eucalyptus, or even garden twigs in winter add organic texture for almost nothing
  • Trays: A piece of flat slate, a chopping board, or a folded linen cloth corrals smaller items tidily
  • Candles: Cream beeswax pillar candles from food shops or pound stores hit the Japandi palette perfectly
  • Wall decor: A large round mirror from a charity shop, spray-painted matte black or left natural, reads as intentional
  • Plants: A single pothos, spider plant or small olive tree in a terracotta pot is Japandi at its most honest
  • Art: Print a botanical ink-wash image at home in black and white and frame it in a simple raw wood frame

What the Experts Say About Japandi Design

Japandi has moved well beyond trend status — it's becoming one of the defining residential interior styles of the decade, and it's easy to see why when you understand what it's actually doing for people's sense of calm at home.

The philosophy at its heart is about reducing visual noise without reducing warmth. That's the balance that makes Japandi so liveable compared to pure minimalism, which can feel cold and aspirational in a way that's exhausting to maintain day to day.

If you want to read more about the history and principles behind the style, Japandi Style: Everything You Need to Know About These East-Meets-West Interiors from Architectural Digest is a genuinely useful deep read — it explains the wabi-sabi and hygge connections in a way that gives you real context for your decor decisions.

The practical upshot for console table styling is this: Japandi design rewards permanence over trend-chasing. The table, the art above it, the ceramic on the surface — buy these things carefully and they'll work just as well in fifteen years as they do today.
